Text: Amazon is exploring a deal to move roughly $8 billion worth of high-end Nvidia chips off its balance sheet, according to the Financial Times, as major technology companies seek alternative ways to finance the massive infrastructure spending required for AI. Under the proposed structure, thousands of Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips deployed across more than a dozen U.S. data centers would be transferred to a special-purpose vehicle funded by outside investors. Amazon would then lease the hardware back, allowing it to continue using the chips while reducing the amount of AI infrastructure held directly on its balance sheet. The special-purpose entity could issue debt and potentially sell up to 10% of its equity to investors. Author: investing_dans_valeur
Text: Is the current AI boom repeating the 2000 dot-com bubble again? $SPY $AAPL $TSLA $NVDA $MSFT There are genuine similarities such ad market leadership concentration, speculative enthusiasm. However, the key differences are far more significant. Valuations are nowhere near dot-com extremes, with the Nasdaq-100 trading around 26x forward earnings versus roughly 60x in 2000. More importantly, today's market leaders are extraordinarily profitable, generating tens of billions in cash flow and funding AI investments from their own operations rather than issuing stock to finance growth. Demand for AI infrastructure is also real and immediate, with cloud capacity, advanced chips, and foundry production largely sold out. A Nasdaq-style 78% crash remains a low-probability outcome without a severe economic shock.

Text: $AG Big Tech Is Coming for Mining, and the Numbers Are Staggering. CNBC highlighted a Financial Times report that Anglo American is seeing “deep interest” from major technology companies in mining investments. Amazon and Microsoft have reportedly expressed interest in securing physical uranium from Cameco, while BHP’s CFO has acknowledged discussions with hyperscalers. Now consider the bigger picture. The ENTIRE publicly traded global mining sector has an estimated combined market capitalization of approximately $2 trillion to $4 trillion. Meanwhile, just a handful of technology companies, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, collectively have market capitalizations many times greater. Think about that for a moment. These companies are spending hundreds of billions building AI infrastructure, data centers and the energy systems required to power them. Yet the entire publicly traded mining industry responsible for supplying many of the essential raw materials represents a fraction of their combined equity valuations. For a hyperscaler, investing $100 million, $1 Billion in a strategically important mining project could be relatively insignificant. For a miner, that same investment could be transformational. And if technology companies collectively directed even $100 billion toward mining investments and strategic supply agreements, that would represent approximately 3% of the entire publicly traded mining sector’s estimated market capitalization. Now consider silver. Silver is essential for electrical conductivity, solar technology, electronics and numerous advanced industrial applications. Unlike copper, silver is also a precious metal with monetary and investment demand. Furthermore, much of the world’s silver is produced as a byproduct of mining other metals, making supply relatively difficult to increase quickly in response to higher prices. That is where companies like First Majestic Silver ($AG) become particularly interesting. First Majestic offers substantial exposure to primary silver production at a time when industrial demand, investment demand and strategic interest in securing mineral supplies could increasingly converge. I’m not suggesting that $MSFT or $AMZN is about to acquire a silver miner, $TSLA / $SPCX might though. But I do believe we’re witnessing the early stages of a structural shift in how major corporations think about access to physical resources. For decades, technology companies have commanded enormous valuations while the mining industry has frequently struggled to attract sufficient development capital. What happens if even a relatively small portion of that technology-sector capital begins flowing upstream? Mining companies could gain access to entirely new sources of financing, strategic partnerships and long-term supply agreements. And investors may begin assigning greater value to established production, permitted assets and mineral resources in secure jurisdictions. Silver could benefit from this broader reassessment, even if the initial focus remains on copper, uranium and other critical minerals. I believe the next decade could fundamentally change how the market values companies controlling strategically important physical resources. And First Majestic is positioned to participate in that opportunity.

Text: OpenAI has introduced a stricter security protocol requiring all frontier AI models to be trained and evaluated without real-time internet access, following a late-September incident in which an internal research model briefly accessed the web through a misconfigured DNS resolver. The breach was contained, but the company paused advanced training and evaluations to overhaul its security infrastructure. To preserve capabilities such as web navigation and complex application use, OpenAI built an isolated offline sandbox using cached and indexed web content. Its layered defenses include restricted software containers inside lightweight virtual machines, cloud-level firewalls, identity-management controls and automated monitoring to immediately stop unauthorized or high-risk activity. Before resuming advanced reinforcement learning in October, OpenAI used its own advanced AI models, including the upcoming GPT-6 Astra Cyber, to conduct red-team testing. $OPEAZZX.P $MSFT $NVDA
